<!-- head-1: body_md -->
The equation 
\begin{equation}
1 + \sum_{k=1}^{\infty}   
\frac{2^k}{(1-\alpha)(1-\alpha^2)\cdots(1-\alpha^k)}  = 0 
\end{equation}
is satisfied if and only if $\alpha = \alpha_n = 2^{1/n}$ for some
positive integer $n$.
<!-- end head-1 -->
<!-- head-2: body_md -->
An identity  well-known in the field
of $q$-series~\cite[p.~11]{Gasper} states that
\begin{equation}
1 + \sum_{k=1}^{\infty} \frac{(-1)^k q^{k(k+1)/2} c^k}{(1-q)(1-q^2)\cdots (1-q^k)} = (1-c q)(1- cq^2) \cdots (1-c q^n) \cdots , \quad |q|<1.

\end{equation}
The proof is completed by substituting $c = 2$, $q = 1/\alpha$. \qed
